title: Ionic & Covalent Bonding
description: Ionic bonding by electron transfer between Group I/II metals and Group VI/VII non-metals, covalent bonding in simple molecules, dot-and-cross diagrams, and linking structure type to properties — Core tier of IGCSE Chemistry 0620.

notes.heading: Two Routes to a Full Outer Shell
notes.body:
0620 questions usually open by asking you to STATE the type of bonding from the elements involved — so make the decision rule automatic.

📌 Definitions
• **Ionic bond**: formed when a METAL atom transfers electrons to a NON-METAL atom; the oppositely charged ions then attract each other strongly.
• **Covalent bond**: a pair of electrons SHARED between two NON-METAL atoms.

🔑 How to decide (the exam rule)
• Metal + non-metal → ionic.
• Non-metal + non-metal → covalent.
Both routes give each atom a full outer shell — the electron configuration of a noble gas — which is why atoms bond at all.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Describing ionic bonding as 'sharing'. Transfer = ionic; sharing = covalent. Mark schemes reject 'sharing' in an ionic answer even if the rest is correct.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Metals are on the left of the Periodic Table (Groups I, II); the reactive non-metals are on the right (Groups VI, VII).
• After bonding, every atom involved has a full outer shell.

notes.heading: Ionic Bonding: Electron Transfer
notes.body:
Core 0620 expects ionic bonding between Group I or II metals and Group VI or VII non-metals — work from the electronic configurations every time.

🔑 How it works — sodium chloride
Na (2,8,1) loses its 1 outer electron → Na⁺ (2,8). Cl (2,8,7) gains that electron → Cl⁻ (2,8,8). The strong ELECTROSTATIC ATTRACTION between the oppositely charged ions is the ionic bond.

🔑 Getting the ratio right
The total positive charge must balance the total negative charge:
• Mg (2,8,2) has 2 electrons to give away, but each Cl can only take 1 → one Mg bonds with TWO Cl atoms → MgCl₂.
• Two Na atoms are needed to supply the 2 electrons one O atom wants → Na₂O.
• Ca (2,8,8,2) gives 2 electrons to one O atom → CaO.

💡 Worked Example
Magnesium + chlorine: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻; each Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻. One Mg²⁺ balances two Cl⁻, formula MgCl₂.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing MgCl or NaO. Count the electrons that must be transferred, then match donors to acceptors.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Metal loses, non-metal gains; both end with a full outer shell.
• Charges on the ions tell you the formula: balance + and − to zero.

notes.heading: Dot-and-Cross Diagrams for Ionic Compounds
notes.body:
You will be asked to DRAW these, so learn the marking conventions exactly.

🔑 The rules
• Show the OUTER SHELL only (inner shells are not drawn).
• Use dots for one element's electrons and crosses for the other's.
• Draw each ion inside square brackets and write its charge OUTSIDE the bracket, top right: [Na]⁺ and [Cl]⁻.
• The transferred electron keeps its original symbol, so the diagram shows where every electron came from.

💡 Worked Example — NaCl
Na starts with 1 outer electron (a cross); Cl starts with 7 outer electrons (dots). After transfer, [Na]⁺ has an empty outer shell position (its new outer shell is full at 8) and [Cl]⁻ shows 7 dots + 1 cross = 8 electrons. For MgCl₂ draw TWO chloride ions, each having gained one of magnesium's electrons — and write no charge on the Mg²⁺ bracket other than 2+.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting the brackets and charges — without them the diagram shows atoms, not ions, and scores zero for the diagram mark.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Outer shell only, dots and crosses, brackets, charges.
• Every ion shown must have a full outer shell.

illustration.alt: Dot-and-cross diagram of a sodium atom transferring its outer electron to a chlorine atom, forming bracketed Na+ and Cl- ions with full outer shells.
illustration.caption: The transferred electron keeps its own symbol: Cl⁻ shows chlorine's 7 crosses plus sodium's dot, inside brackets with the charge outside.

notes.heading: Covalent Bonding: Sharing Pairs of Electrons
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A covalent bond is a SHARED PAIR of electrons between two non-metal atoms. Each atom contributes one electron to the pair, and both atoms count the shared pair towards their outer shell.

🔑 The Core molecule set — learn to draw each one
• **H₂**: each H shares 1 electron → 1 shared pair; each H now has a full shell of 2.
• **Cl₂**: each Cl (2,8,7) shares 1 electron → 1 shared pair; each Cl now has 8 in its outer shell.
• **HCl**: H shares with Cl → 1 shared pair; H has 2, Cl has 8.

💡 Worked Example — counting electrons in Cl₂
Each chlorine brings 7 outer electrons. One electron from each is shared (the bonding pair), leaving 3 unshared pairs — called LONE PAIRS — on each Cl. Total around each Cl: 3 lone pairs + 1 bonding pair = 8 electrons.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Counting the shared pair for only one of the two atoms. A shared pair belongs to BOTH atoms' outer shells at the same time — that is the whole point of sharing.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• One shared pair = one covalent bond (a single bond).
• Hydrogen is full with 2 electrons; the other atoms in this topic aim for 8.

notes.heading: Covalent Molecules: H₂O, CH₄ and NH₃
notes.body:
🔑 How to build each dot-and-cross diagram
Count the outer electrons each atom must gain to fill its shell — that is the number of bonds it forms.
• **H₂O**: O (2,6) needs 2 → forms 2 bonds, one with each H. Oxygen ends with 2 bonding pairs + 2 lone pairs = 8 outer electrons.
• **CH₄**: C (2,4) needs 4 → forms 4 bonds, one with each H. Carbon has 4 bonding pairs, no lone pairs.
• **NH₃**: N (2,5) needs 3 → forms 3 bonds, one with each H. Nitrogen ends with 3 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair = 8 outer electrons.

💡 Worked Example — checking NH₃
Total electrons shown around N: 3 shared pairs (6 electrons, counted for N) + 1 lone pair (2 electrons) = 8 ✓. Each H sees its 1 shared pair = 2 electrons ✓.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Drawing NH₃ with a fourth bond or H₂O with the two lone pairs missing. The lone pairs still belong in the diagram — examiners check for them.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Bonds formed = electrons needed to complete the outer shell: H needs 1, O needs 2, N needs 3, C needs 4.
• Check: every atom (except H, which wants 2) should reach 8 outer electrons.

notes.heading: Properties: Ionic vs Simple Covalent
notes.body:
0620 Core asks you to STATE properties from the structure type — learn the table and the two key explanations.

📌 Ionic compounds (e.g. NaCl, MgCl₂)
• HIGH melting and boiling points — the strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions act throughout the whole structure, so a lot of energy is needed to separate the ions.
• Do NOT conduct electricity when SOLID — the ions are held in fixed positions.
• DO conduct when MOLTEN or DISSOLVED in water (aqueous) — the ions are free to move and carry the charge.
• Usually soluble in water.

📌 Simple covalent substances (e.g. CH₄, H₂O, Cl₂)
• LOW melting and boiling points — only the weak forces BETWEEN the small molecules need to be overcome; the covalent bonds inside each molecule are not broken.
• Do NOT conduct electricity in any state — no ions and no free electrons.
• Usually insoluble in water (some exceptions, e.g. sugar).

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying 'the covalent bonds are weak' to explain a low melting point. The covalent bonds are STRONG; melting or boiling a simple molecular substance never breaks them — it separates the molecules from each other.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Conduction always needs charged particles that can MOVE: mobile ions (molten/aqueous ionic) or delocalised electrons (metals, graphite).
• High melting point + conducts when molten but not solid → ionic. Low melting point + never conducts → simple covalent.

notes.heading: Diamond and Graphite
notes.body:
Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon — giant covalent structures whose different bonding arrangements give opposite properties. Relating each property to the structure is the exam skill.

🔑 Diamond
Each carbon atom forms 4 covalent bonds to 4 other carbon atoms, building a rigid 3D tetrahedral network.
• VERY HARD — every bond must be broken to scratch it (used in cutting tools and drill tips).
• Very high melting point.
• Does NOT conduct electricity — all 4 outer electrons of every carbon are locked in bonds; there are no free charge carriers.

🔑 Graphite
Each carbon atom forms only 3 covalent bonds, giving flat layers of hexagons; the 4th outer electron of each carbon is DELOCALISED between the layers.
• SOFT and slippery — the layers can slide over each other (used as a lubricant and in pencil 'lead').
• CONDUCTS electricity — the delocalised electrons can move along the layers (used for electrodes).

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying graphite is soft 'because its bonds are weak'. The covalent bonds within the layers are just as strong as diamond's; it is the forces BETWEEN the layers that are weak.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Diamond: 4 bonds per carbon, hard, non-conductor. Graphite: 3 bonds per carbon, slippery, conductor.
• Same element, different structure, different properties — always link the property to the bonding.

flashcards.definition: The strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed when a metal transfers electrons to a non-metal.
flashcards.example: Na (2,8,1) gives 1 electron to Cl (2,8,7), forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻.

flashcards.definition: A shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms; each atom contributes one electron to the pair.
flashcards.example: In Cl₂ each chlorine shares one electron, so both reach 8 outer electrons.

flashcards.definition: Shows outer shells only, with dots for one element's electrons and crosses for the other's; ions drawn in brackets with the charge outside.
flashcards.example: [Na]⁺ and [Cl]⁻ — the chloride shows 7 crosses plus the 1 dot it gained from sodium.

flashcards.definition: The total positive charge must equal the total negative charge, giving the ratio of ions in the formula.
flashcards.example: Mg²⁺ needs two Cl⁻, so magnesium chloride is MgCl₂.

flashcards.definition: A pair of outer-shell electrons not involved in bonding.
flashcards.example: In NH₃, nitrogen has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair; in H₂O, oxygen has 2 of each.

flashcards.term: Why ionic compounds have high melting points
flashcards.definition: Strong electrostatic forces act between oppositely charged ions throughout the structure, so a lot of energy is needed to separate them.
flashcards.example: NaCl melts at 801 °C, while methane melts at −182 °C.

flashcards.definition: Ionic compounds conduct electricity only when molten or aqueous, because then the ions are free to move; in the solid the ions are fixed.
flashcards.example: Solid NaCl does not conduct; molten NaCl does.

flashcards.definition: A substance made of small molecules with strong covalent bonds inside the molecules but only weak forces between them.
flashcards.example: CH₄, H₂O and Cl₂ — low melting points and no electrical conduction.

flashcards.term: Why simple covalent substances have low melting points
flashcards.definition: Only the weak forces between the molecules need to be overcome; the strong covalent bonds inside the molecules are not broken.
flashcards.example: Boiling water separates H₂O molecules — the O–H bonds stay intact.

flashcards.definition: Giant covalent form of carbon: each carbon bonded to 4 others in a tetrahedral network. Very hard, very high melting point, does not conduct electricity.
flashcards.example: Used in cutting tools and drill tips because it is the hardest natural substance.

flashcards.definition: Giant covalent form of carbon: each carbon bonded to 3 others in hexagonal layers, with delocalised electrons between the layers.
flashcards.example: Soft and slippery (lubricant, pencil lead) and conducts electricity (electrodes).

flashcards.definition: Each carbon bonds to only 3 others, leaving one outer electron per atom delocalised and free to move along the layers.
flashcards.example: In diamond all 4 outer electrons are held in bonds, so diamond cannot conduct.

choices: The strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
A shared pair of electrons between two atoms
The attraction between metal ions and delocalised electrons
A weak force between two molecules
questions.explanation: Ionic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between the positive and negative ions formed by electron transfer. A shared pair of electrons describes a covalent bond.

questions.stem: Which pair of elements reacts to form an ionic compound?
choices: Hydrogen and chlorine
Carbon and oxygen
Nitrogen and hydrogen
Sodium and chlorine
questions.explanation: Ionic bonding forms between a metal and a non-metal: sodium is a Group I metal and chlorine a Group VII non-metal. The other three pairs are non-metal + non-metal, so they bond covalently.

choices: The transfer of electrons from one atom to another
A pair of electrons shared between two non-metal atoms
The attraction between two oppositely charged ions
A sea of delocalised electrons around positive ions
questions.explanation: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons; each non-metal atom contributes one electron and both count the pair towards a full outer shell. Transfer describes ionic bonding.

questions.stem: Which form of carbon conducts electricity?
choices: Diamond
Neither diamond nor graphite
Graphite
Both diamond and graphite equally
questions.explanation: In graphite each carbon forms only 3 bonds, leaving one delocalised electron per atom free to move along the layers. In diamond all 4 outer electrons are locked in covalent bonds, so it cannot conduct.

questions.stem: When magnesium (2,8,2) reacts with chlorine (2,8,7), how many electrons does each magnesium atom lose, and how many chlorine atoms does it supply?
choices: 1 electron; 1 chlorine atom
2 electrons; 2 chlorine atoms
2 electrons; 1 chlorine atom
1 electron; 2 chlorine atoms
questions.explanation: Mg loses both its outer electrons to reach 2,8, but each Cl atom can accept only one (to reach 2,8,8). So one Mg supplies two Cl atoms, giving MgCl₂.

questions.stem: In a dot-and-cross diagram of sodium chloride, how many electrons are shown in the outer shell of the chloride ion?
questions.explanation: Chlorine's 7 outer electrons plus the 1 electron gained from sodium give a full shell of 8 — 7 crosses and 1 dot, drawn inside brackets with a − charge.

questions.stem: How many shared pairs of electrons are there in a molecule of methane, CH₄?
questions.explanation: Carbon (2,4) needs 4 electrons, so it shares one pair with each of the 4 hydrogen atoms — 4 shared pairs (4 single bonds). Carbon reaches 8 outer electrons; each H reaches 2.

questions.stem: In a dot-and-cross diagram of water, H₂O, how many bonding pairs and how many lone pairs are on the oxygen atom?
choices: 1 bonding pair and 3 lone pairs
2 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair
2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs
4 bonding pairs and no lone pairs
questions.explanation: Oxygen (2,6) forms 2 bonds (one with each H) and keeps 4 of its own electrons as 2 lone pairs: 2 bonding pairs + 2 lone pairs = 8 outer electrons. The lone pairs must be drawn for full marks.

questions.stem: Why does solid sodium chloride NOT conduct electricity, while molten sodium chloride does?
choices: In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions; when molten the ions are free to move and carry the charge
Molten NaCl contains a sea of free electrons
Solid NaCl contains no charged particles
Heating converts the ionic bonds into covalent bonds
questions.explanation: Conduction needs charged particles that can move. The ions exist in the solid but are locked in place; melting releases them to flow towards the electrodes. Metals conduct with electrons — ionic compounds conduct with ions.

questions.stem: In an ammonia molecule, NH₃, how many electrons in total are in the outer shell of the nitrogen atom (counting shared electrons)?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen forms 3 bonding pairs (shared with the 3 H atoms, all counted for N) and keeps 1 lone pair: 6 + 2 = 8 outer electrons — a full shell.

questions.stem: Sodium chloride melts at 801 °C but methane, CH₄, melts at −182 °C. What explains this difference?
choices: NaCl contains strong covalent bonds while the bonds in CH₄ are weak
CH₄ is ionic, so it melts more easily
Strong electrostatic forces act between the ions throughout NaCl, whereas only weak forces between the small CH₄ molecules need to be overcome
NaCl molecules are larger than CH₄ molecules
questions.explanation: Melting NaCl means separating ions held by strong electrostatic forces throughout the structure; melting methane only separates molecules from each other — the strong C–H covalent bonds inside each molecule are untouched.

questions.stem: Graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not, even though both are pure carbon. Why?
choices: Graphite has weaker covalent bonds than diamond
In graphite each carbon bonds to only 3 others, leaving delocalised electrons free to move; in diamond all 4 outer electrons per carbon are held in covalent bonds
Diamond is held together by ionic bonds
Graphite contains metal ions between its layers
questions.explanation: Conduction needs mobile charge carriers. Graphite's 4th outer electron per carbon is delocalised between the layers and can flow; diamond has no free electrons because every outer electron is locked in a bond.

questions.stem: A white solid melts at about 800 °C. It does not conduct electricity when solid, but its aqueous solution conducts. What type of bonding does it contain?
choices: Ionic
Simple covalent
Giant covalent
Metallic
questions.explanation: High melting point plus the solid/molten conductivity switch is the fingerprint of an ionic compound: ions fixed when solid, mobile when molten or dissolved. Simple covalent substances melt far lower and never conduct; metals conduct when solid.

questions.stem: In a dot-and-cross diagram of a chlorine molecule, Cl₂, how many lone pairs are there on EACH chlorine atom?
questions.explanation: Each Cl starts with 7 outer electrons: 1 is used in the shared bonding pair, leaving 6 electrons = 3 lone pairs per atom. Total around each Cl: 3 lone pairs + 1 bonding pair = 8.

questions.stem: Calcium (2,8,8,2) reacts with oxygen (2,6) to form calcium oxide, CaO. Which statement describes the bonding correctly?
choices: Calcium gains 2 electrons to form Ca²⁺
Calcium loses 2 electrons to form Ca²⁺ (2,8,8) and oxygen gains them to form O²⁻ (2,8)
Calcium and oxygen share 2 pairs of electrons in a double covalent bond
Calcium loses 1 electron to form Ca⁺
questions.explanation: Metal + non-metal → electron transfer. Ca loses both its outer electrons (2,8,8) and O needs exactly 2 to complete its shell (2,8): one Ca²⁺ balances one O²⁻, giving the formula CaO.
